# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). content.text:
Based on the codebase, the `dormant` repo setting is read by:

**1. The scheduler** (`packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/scheduler-run.mjs:550`)
   - Stops before evaluating any preconditions when a repo is dormant
   - Prevents work item instantiation, agent sessions, and maintenance PRs

**2. The executor** (`packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/executor.mjs:740`)
   - Checks dormancy to avoid processing queued work items

**3. Fleet machinery** (`packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/`):
   - **check-fleet-roster.mjs** — Skips reading freshness verdict for dormant members; closes any drift issues as *not planned*
   - **check-fleet-pack-seeds.mjs** — Excludes dormant repos from pack seed checks
   - **scan-for-needed-packs.mjs** — Skips dormant repos when scanning
   - **force-add-packs.mjs** — Skips dormant repos when adding missing packs
   - **force-fleet-baseline.mjs** — Excludes dormant repos from baseline forcing (unless `--include-dormant` flag)

**4. Task signals** (`packs/claudinite-tasks/signals/fleet.mjs:69,151`)
   - Tracks dormant status in fleet reports and filters dormant repos from task signal processing

The `isDormant` predicate is deliberately **re-exported from the engine** (`engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs:170`) so the fleet sweep uses the *exact same definition* the repo's own scheduler does — preventing the fleet from nagging repos that have explicitly opted out of recurring work.

content.text:
I've read the three paths this touches. Here's my answer to your closing question, then two decisions I need from you.

**On firing the scheduler instead of reading the setting — I'd keep the read.** Four reasons:

1. **A dormant scheduler exits clean today, deliberately.** `scheduler-run.mjs:550` prints its notice and returns 0. The basics rule is explicit that an expected, handled outcome exits clean and non-zero is reserved for genuine breakage. Reading dormancy off a *failed* state means making dormancy fail — inverting that rule and leaving every dormant member's Actions tab permanently red.

2. **The dispatch is the work dormancy exists to stop.** The declaration's whole promise is that nothing scheduled runs for nothing on a repo nobody is working on. A sweep that fires every member's scheduler to learn whether it should have fired it spends exactly the Actions minutes that were opted out of.

3. **A dispatch is not a result.** 204 means queued, so each member then needs polling to a terminal state — minutes per member per sweep, against one small file fetch today. `check-fleet-roster` and the two pack-seed scans are read-only sweeps; there's no reason for them to become write-side operations.

4. **It doesn't actually remove the second reader.** Shepherd would still have to distinguish "dormant" from "no work due" from "workflow disabled" from "token missing" — that's a parsing contract over log text, strictly worse than one shared predicate over a declared boolean.

What I think *did* prompt the question is real, though: once the setting moves into pack config, Shepherd has to know two locations, and the standing rule is that a reader of member config resolves the new key and every legacy spelling permanently. The fix for that is one exported accessor in the engine owning both locations — which is the shape `isDormant` already has — so Shepherd never learns there were two.

Your instinct is right in exactly one place: `force-fleet-baseline.mjs` already dispatches. There the pre-filter is belt-and-braces, since the member's own scheduler self-skips anyway.

**The tension I want to flag before building:** a dormant repo's scheduler is what runs the update task. If the fan-out still skips dormant members (as you asked), then "X days behind on engine version" becomes a signal that drifts forever and nothing can clear.

input.title: Move `dormant` out of engine settings into the claudinite-tasks pack — dormancy is a scheduler property, not a repo property
input.body:
## Problem

`dormant` is declared as a top-level key of `.claudinite-settings.json` and validated by the engine's `loadConfig` (`engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs`), with `isDormant` exported from there. That places it among the engine's general settings, where it reads as a property of *the repository*.

It is not. Every one of its effects is about **the scheduler**: the queue stops instantiating, the executor stops picking up, and the fleet sweeps stop expecting movement. A repo with no `claudinite-tasks` declaration has no scheduler at all, and `dormant` means nothing there — yet the engine still accepts and validates the key for it.

The consequence shows up in Shepherd: because dormancy is modelled as a repo property, `check-fleet-roster.mjs` drops a dormant member out of the freshness half entirely (`entry.dormant || …` at the freshness gate). A dormant member's mount can drift arbitrarily far behind canon and the roster reports nothing at all about it.

## The end state

`dormant` becomes a parameter of the `claudinite-tasks` pack entry:

```json
{ "id": "claudinite-tasks", "config": { "dormant": true } }
```

The predicate moves to `packs/claudinite-tasks/shared-code/dormancy.mjs` — the tasks pack's published cross-pack surface, which the `pack-independence` barrier already names as importable. The engine stops knowing the word: no `CONFIG_KEYS` entry, no validation, no `dormant` field on the loaded config, no `isDormant` export. The scheduler, the executor, the dashboard and Shepherd all read the one predicate from the pack that owns the mechanism.

One predicate, both shapes, as today: a raw parsed declaration (how a cross-repo reader sees another member) and the normalized config `loadConfig` returns. A second notion of dormancy would nag exactly the repos that had already opted out.

## Owner decisions taken

**Where Shepherd learns dormancy — hybrid.** Read-only sweeps (`fleet-roster`, `fleet-pack-seeds`, `scan-for-needed-packs`) keep reading the declaration: they are cheap, side-effect-free, and firing a member's scheduler to learn whether it should have been fired is the exact recurring work dormancy exists to stop. Fan-outs that *already* dispatch the scheduler drop their pre-filter and let the member's own scheduler self-skip, recording what it reported — one authority rather than two.

Rejected: dropping the declaration read entirely in favour of dispatching every member's scheduler and reading a failed state. A dormant scheduler exits **clean** by this repo's own convention (an expected, handled outcome exits clean; non-zero is for genuine breakage), so that model requires making dormancy fail — painting every dormant member's Actions tab permanently red — and it replaces one small file read per member with a dispatch plus polling to a terminal state.

**A dormant member behind on the engine version — reported, advisory only.** The freshness half now measures dormant members and reports their drift. The fan-out still leaves them alone, so the signal is information for the owner rather than something the fleet acts on; it clears by waking the repo or an explicit include-dormant run. What stops being reported is *scheduler inactivity*: a dormant scheduler that is not running is obeying its declaration, and the roster must not call that unhealthy.

## Scope

- [ ] `packs/claudinite-tasks/shared-code/dormancy.mjs` — the predicate and its settings-error reporting, reading the pack-entry config with the legacy top-level key still resolved
- [ ] Engine: drop `dormant` from `CONFIG_KEYS`, the returned shape and the exported predicate; tolerate the legacy key so a member carrying it does not get an unknown-setting error
- [ ] Scheduler and executor read the pack's predicate
- [ ] Shepherd: dormancy reported as scheduler state, not repo health; dormant members measured for freshness; `fleet-baseline` drops its pre-filter and lets the scheduler self-skip
- [ ] Dashboard: the work block hides its tasks elements when the scheduler is dormant
- [ ] Migration record moving the key from the top level into the pack entry
- [ ] Tests for each, seen failing first

**Where Shepherd learns dormancy — hybrid.** Read-only sweeps (`fleet-roster`, `fleet-pack-seeds`, `scan-for-needed-packs`) keep reading the declaration: they are cheap, side-effect-free, and firing a member's scheduler to learn whether it should have been fired is the exact recurring work dormancy exists to stop. Fan-outs that *already* dispatch the scheduler drop their pre-filter and let the member's own scheduler self-skip, recording what it reported — one authority rather than two.

Rejected: dropping the declaration read entirely in favour of dispatching every member's scheduler and reading a failed state. A dormant scheduler exits **clean** by this repo's own convention (an expected, handled outcome exits clean; non-zero is for genuine breakage), so that model requires making dormancy fail — painting every dormant member's Actions tab permanently red — and it replaces one small file read per member with a dispatch plus polling to a terminal state.

**A dormant member behind on the engine version — reported, advisory only.** The freshness half now measures dormant members and reports their drift. The fan-out still leaves them alone, so the signal is information for the owner rather than something the fleet acts on; it clears by waking the repo or an explicit include-dormant run. What stops being reported is *scheduler inactivity*: a dormant scheduler that is not running is obeying its declaration, and the roster must not call that unhealthy.

## Scope

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/shared-code/dormancy.mjs` — the predicate and its settings-error reporting, reading the pack-entry config with the legacy top-level key still resolved
- Engine: drop `dormant` from `CONFIG_KEYS`, the returned shape and the exported predicate; tolerate the legacy key so a member carrying it does not get an unknown-setting error
- Scheduler and executor read the pack's predicate
- Shepherd: dormancy reported as scheduler state, not repo health; dormant members measured for freshness; `fleet-baseline` drops its pre-filter and lets the scheduler self-skip
- Dashboard: the work block hides its tasks elements when the scheduler is dormant
- Migration record moving the key from the top level into the pack entry
- Tests for each, seen failing first

input.title: Retire the top-level `dormant` tolerance once the fleet has converged onto the pack-entry spelling
input.body:
#1845 moves `dormant` from a top-level key of `.claudinite-settings.json` into the `claudinite-tasks` pack entry's `config`. While the fleet converges, two things stay in place:

- `packs/claudinite-tasks/dormancy.mjs` resolves the top-level key underneath the pack-entry one, so a member that has not yet run the migration record still reads as dormant.
- `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs` keeps `dormant` among its legacy keys, so a member still carrying it does not get an unknown-setting error.

Both come out together. Removing either alone is worse than removing neither: the reader without the settings tolerance turns a stale member's declaration into a hard settings error, and the tolerance without the reader silently flips a dormant member awake.

## When

One convergence window after the migration record ships — the time a member converging nightly needs to receive the record and have it rewrite its declaration. Gated on that window, never on a census of members: the canon cannot see which repos are active, inert or long stale, so "no member still declares it at the top level" is a condition nothing can ever answer, and until it is answered the tolerance stands forever.

## What removing it looks like

- Drop the top-level fallback in `dormantValue` and its `@legacy-tolerance` marker.
- Drop `dormant` from `LEGACY_CONFIG_KEYS` in the engine.
- A member that somehow still carries the top-level key then gets the unknown-setting error, which is the correct end state: the key means nothing there.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/writing-tests

# Testing practices

A consuming repo's own test *mechanics* — runner, layout, which suites exist — are its own docs'; CI-trigger rules and the `GITHUB_TOKEN` workflow-recursion gotcha are [git-github-advanced](../../../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md)'s.

- See a test fail before you trust it: write it red before the fix (green after), or break what it guards and watch it go red. A test that has never failed proves nothing. For a **refusal/negative** test — one asserting a guard yields *nothing* — the write-it-red-first branch is unavailable: the pre-change code also yielded nothing, so the test passes from birth and proves nothing. See-it-fail there **must** be the second method — mutate the new guard (weaken it), watch the test bite, then restore it. Restore with `git checkout -- <file>` (or `git stash`) taken at the moment of mutating — never a `.bak` copy saved earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in between and silently discards that intervening work. If the mutation was **staged** (to make a check that scans `git diff --cached` fire), a bare `git checkout -- <file>` restores from the index — which now holds the mutation — so the "restore" is a no-op; use `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` (or `git reset` first).
- A mechanism meant to survive a retry, re-queue, or hand-off needs a test that calls it twice, not once. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case corrupts state — the double-call is what a real retry, requeue, or hand-off actually does. When the mechanism arbitrates by identity (a claim, a lock), the second call must come from a **different actor**: a single actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an identity-masked race, since it still recognizes its own claim as valid.
- A simulator of a stateful mechanism must advance state only where the real engine's code actually leaves a mark — never wherever the rule's stated description says a transition happens. A sim that fires on every event matching the rule's *intent* is correct by construction against that rule and blind to exactly the silent paths where the real implementation and the rule have quietly diverged — which is where a genuine bug usually lives. Read the real engine's code for what it *writes*, and model that.
- Before trusting a new transform/normalizer, run it over the *real existing corpus* it will process, not just hand-picked test inputs — the live data exposes edge cases your examples won't. Relatedly, prefer a generic structural rule over a hand-maintained list of special cases: the enumerated list needs per-instance upkeep and silently has gaps, while a rule keyed on structure (e.g. "a known registry label under any 2-letter ccTLD") covers the whole class at once. (3)
- A test that stubs the exact boundary where the bug lives can't catch that bug — it guards only the shape it asserts, not the runtime effect. Say what it can't catch.
- A test that dereferences a path inside a **read-only dependency tree someone else refreshes** — a vendored mount, a synced submodule, generated output from an upstream build — is a test whose fixture a stranger can delete: the day upstream retires that file the case fails `ENOENT` with nothing in your repo having changed. Assert against a path only when the test itself creates it; when a case genuinely needs an upstream file, read it **defensively** and skip with a stated reason if it is gone, so a retirement upstream reports as "no longer applicable" rather than as your repo being broken. Check what actually runs these cases too — a suite that the repo's own gate never invokes reports its breakage to whoever happens to look.
- **Never test that a value is set.** A test that reads a value someone declared — a config or manifest field (`assert.equal(task.expected_outcome, 'fresh_pr')`), an exported constant or default object (`assert.deepEqual(DEFAULTS, {…})`), a settings file naming a pack, a workflow's `run:` line, a frontmatter key — and asserts it is the literal it was set to restates the file under test in a second file. It can only fail when someone changes the value **on purpose**, so it catches no defect and instead taxes every deliberate change with a mirrored edit — and teaches that the value is load-bearing prose to be restated, which is how one setting ends up copied into a comment, a worker doc, a README table and a test, so flipping it becomes a five-file diff. The see-it-fail test exposes it: to make the assertion go red you must break the thing it asserts, which is not a bug. "It exists", "it has the right shape" and "it is one of these" are the same test in a looser coat. Test the **behaviour the value drives** instead: feed the real code the declared value and assert what the code does with it — a task declared `weekly` is planned once across a fourteen-day clock, a check declared over `**/*.mjs` fires on a fixture `.mjs` and stays silent on a `.md`, a default object yields the documented output when nothing overrides it. Where no code reads the value there is nothing to test; if a declaration genuinely must not change without deliberation, that is a review concern, not a test. What *does* earn an assertion on declared data is a claim spanning two artifacts that could drift independently: the doc a field *names* exists; every signal the code reads is declared; two implementations of the same list agree; a value the runtime constrains is inside its legal set — proven by running the constraint, not by re-listing the set.
- **Testing a task's precondition or declaration** — assert only the pack's own code: a
  task-local term's decisions, a worker's behaviour, or a composition it designed; a plain
  built-in term or a validated declaration is the scheduler's own mechanism, proved once by its
  own suite.
- Prefer a single shared double; but when a subsystem is faked by more than one (a minimal unit stub vs. a faithful harness that boots the real module), a new call into the faked surface must be taught to **every** double, or the untaught one breaks — and the faithful harness turns an unmodeled API into a confusing **far-away** failure (a DOM-snapshot pixel-diff, not a local error at the call site). After adding a call into a faked boundary, find every double of it and extend each.
- When one wire format, encoding, or algorithm is **implemented twice** — two languages, two tiers, a hand-rolled client encoder against the server's library — no compiler, type system, or single test run spans the two, so the only thing holding them together is a **shared vector set carried deliberately by both suites**: the same inputs and the same expected outputs, asserted independently on each side, including the boundary cases the two could plausibly round differently (a value exactly on a bisection midpoint, a tie, a truncation edge). A vector asserted on only one side is an input nobody ever compared — both suites stay green, in different languages under different runners, while the claim quietly stops covering it. So: touching *either* implementation re-runs *both* suites, and adding a vector adds it to both. Where the pairing is mechanical (the two vector lists must contain the same inputs), pin it with a check rather than a convention.
- A traceability/coverage gate that requires every spec item be *claimed* by some test of one fixed kind proves only that it's claimed, not that it's verified. When items differ in kind, the gate green-lights claims that kind can't check — a pixel snapshot "covers" a click's tab-opening it can never observe, or a state the case never renders (and can't, when the data can't reach it). Segment the gate by the verification each item needs (route behavior to a behavior test, rendering to a snapshot) rather than forcing every item onto one mechanism. (1)
- A golden/snapshot test whose expected artifact is hand-authored to mirror what production renders is a parallel implementation: it drifts from the real output and can't catch changes to the renderer (a hand-built UI gallery even faked a state the app never shows). Drive the snapshot through the real code path, faking only its inputs.
- A snapshot/golden test that depends on the current date/time must inject a fixed reference instant, not read the real clock — else a fixed-date fixture silently rots as wall-clock time passes ("this year" becomes "past" next year). Thread the reference time through the code under test, defaulting to the real clock in production. When retrofitting such a rule into an existing fixture suite, pin the reference instant so existing fixtures land on the same side they were authored for — so only the cases that deliberately exercise the new rule change and the diff stays small and reviewable, rather than a sprawling baseline churn that buries the intended change.
- A round-trip test that asserts by comparing **serialized** forms (`JSON.stringify(decoded) === JSON.stringify(original)`) silently makes key *order* part of the contract: add a field at the top of the encoder's record and append it in the decoder's, and the round-trip fails on ordering alone — with a diff that reads like a data bug and sends you after a value that was correct all along. Deep-equal the parsed structures instead, so the test states what it means; keep serialized comparison only where byte-identity is genuinely the property under test, and say so in the test.
- A new **e2e / heavy-browser** test must go green at least twice in CI before merging — one green run doesn't rule out a flake. This applies only to that class (the real-Chrome `test/fullBrowserHeavyTests/` suites); the deterministic offline/unit/integration tests don't touch a live browser or network, so one green run is enough for them.
- A test that can only run remotely (e.g. CI-only) must diagnose itself: on failure, dump the observed state, not just an assertion. It must also be *hang-proof* — bound every `await` (a timeout race) and set a test-level timeout — so a failure fails fast with that diagnostic instead of burning the whole job's timeout. An unbounded await on something that never settles (e.g. a callback that silently never fires) turns a 5-second failure into a 20-minute hang, and each CI-only iteration already costs a full round-trip.
- Run a suite you know is slow as **its own command with an explicit timeout well above its measured runtime**, and do the dependency install as a *separate, earlier* call. An agent shell caps a command at a default (order of a couple of minutes) and pushes it to the background when it expires; the reflex is then to start the suite over, so one green result costs double the wall clock with two suites racing each other. Chaining setup in front of the suite is what usually pushes the pair past the cap. If a run does get backgrounded, wait on the one already running rather than launching a second.
- To test code that drives a real browser or other external runtime in CI, prefer a *self-authored hermetic input* (e.g. a `data:` URL whose own script reproduces the behavior) over hitting a live third-party target — the live target is non-deterministic and often bot-blocked from a CI/datacenter IP, so it flakes or can't run, while a self-authored input exercises the same engine deterministically. (2)
- Gate a fuzzy quality metric (a coverage %, not a binary pass) behind a high-watermark: refresh the artifact and ratchet the watermark up locally, keep CI read-only (assert against the committed baseline, never rewrite it), and re-baseline by hand only when a deliberate change legitimately moves it — a number that can only climb catches a silent regression without flapping on noise. When the population it covers can *grow* (e.g. new test cases), store the set the watermark was computed over and gate only over the cases shared with it, so a newly added item is excluded rather than dragging the aggregate below the bar; re-anchor the watermark when the set changes. (A single aggregate watermark can then be re-anchored over a regression bundled into the *same* change as a set change — store per-item bars if that must be caught.)
- For behavior a person must sign off on (a third-party integration, an extraction result), keep a layer of declarative, human-reviewed expectation files — distinct from the unit tests, which nobody reads for *intent* — and cover every behavior change with a minimal, representative case there (one behavior per case, no incidental complexity), since that case is what gets reviewed.
- When a snapshot/golden test fails because the output *legitimately* moved (the pixels or bytes changed for a real reason), don't quietly regenerate the baseline to go green — an unreviewed baseline change is an unreviewed behavior change. Surface the diff (committed **expected**, newly-rendered **actual**, highlighted **diff**) and get owner approval before re-baselining; until then keep the *reverted* baseline committed so the branch honestly shows the test red-pending — never commit the new baseline first.
- When a test asserts exact values extracted from a captured artifact (a cached page, a recorded response), record and commit the artifact *first*, then read the expected values off the committed file — don't hand-write the expectations from memory or a live view and hope they match. Guessing the value desyncs the test from the real fixture; reading it off the committed bytes can't.
- A test that maintains a committed artifact should regenerate it into the working tree deterministically (no timestamps, so an unchanged run yields no diff) and skip the write under CI — never shell out to git from a test. Commit the artifact through the normal review flow, like a snapshot.
- Render a UI *image* golden with the engine that matches the surface, and prefer the deterministic one. A surface that is inline-styled SVG, or flexbox-only markup authored for it, renders **bit-exact** through a headless rasterizer (e.g. satori → SVG, resvg → PNG) driven by the shipped code, using **bundled** fonts, never system fonts, and a pinned locale — demand a **zero-pixel** diff there. But that rasterizer has no CSS engine and draws no native widgets: a full shipped page using CSS **grid**, custom properties (`var()`), `@media`, **emoji**, or **form controls** (a range slider, radio, `<select>`) is beyond it — screenshot that with a **headless browser** instead, and allow a *small* diff tolerance (browser antialiasing varies across machines, so it isn't bit-exact). Match the engine to the surface; never reshape the product to fit the rasterizer. (A rasterized popup golden works only because the popup was authored flexbox-only — the moment a surface needs grid/vars/widgets, it needs a browser.) Since the browser goldens aren't gate-able bit-exact and a runner may lack the browser, let those cases **self-skip** where it's absent so the deterministic cases still gate.
- Reproduce a reported golden-image flake with the harness's own pixel comparator, never a raw byte or file-hash compare: a byte-hash is strictly tighter than a zero-pixel-diff comparator (it also fails on identical pixels re-encoded differently), so it manufactures "reproductions" of a flake that never fails the real gate.
- To image-golden a surface your code **injects into a host page** (a control mounted into a third-party toolbar), render it against a **committed capture of the real host DOM with its computed styles flattened inline** — the deterministic rasterizer reads only inline styles, and the host's own stylesheet is not yours to ship. Mount it with the **shipped injector** (so the golden proves the placement, not a hand-placed copy), and name the model's boundary honestly: substituted icon-font glyphs, an approximated host chrome (a captured sample is spec, not folklore — the origin lesson of a supported-targets matrix).

# Running the suite

+// there, and an engine that validated it for such a repo was answering for a mechanism

+//     canon is still behind, and is still reported as behind.

# Writing a check that scans the repo

- **Choosing the file set** — take it from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with

  [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs);

  Strip in **both** directions — a comment that documents or warns about the banned pattern is
  exactly where a naive check trips over its own reasoning, so a commented-out instance must not
  count as present either.

  synthetic clean fixture — a fixture spelling the same gap the check has just keeps proving the

1	// Is this project's SCHEDULER dormant? A project goes dormant when it is finished,
2	// parked, or simply not being worked on: it should stop paying the upkeep of a project
3	// that IS being worked on.
4	//
5	// WHY THIS LIVES IN THIS PACK. Every effect dormancy has is an effect on the queue —
6	// nothing is instantiated, nothing is picked up, and nothing outside expects movement.
7	// A repo that declares no tasks pack has no scheduler at all, so the word means nothing
8	// there, and an engine that validated it for such a repo was answering for a mechanism
9	// it does not own. So the setting is one of this pack's parameters, declared where the
10	// pack is:
11	//
12	//   { "id": "claudinite-tasks", "config": { "dormant": true } }
13	//
14	// What dormancy means, exactly — it is narrow on purpose:
15	//   - NO RECURRING WORK. The vendored scheduler stops before it evaluates a
16	//     precondition, so no work item is instantiated, no agent session is started, and
17	//     no maintenance PR is opened. Nothing scheduled runs "for nothing" on a repo
18	//     nobody is working on.
19	//   - NO SCHEDULER CEREMONY FROM OUTSIDE. Whatever looks at this repo from the outside
20	//     reads the same declaration and does not report a stopped scheduler as unhealthy —
21	//     a scheduler TOLD to stop must not then be nagged for stopping. It says nothing
22	//     about the repo's other health: a dormant member whose mount has fallen behind
23	//     canon is still behind, and is still reported as behind.
24	//   - EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS ON. Claudinite is not switched off: the session hooks, the
25	//     checks engine, the mounted skills and pack prose all work exactly as before the
26	//     moment someone opens a session on the repo. Dormancy is about unattended upkeep,
27	//     never about what an interactive session may do.
28	//
29	// ONE PREDICATE, EVERY SHAPE. It reads a raw parsed .claudinite-settings.json and the
30	// normalized config `loadConfig` returns, because a cross-repo reader fetches another
31	// repo's declaration over the API with no engine loaded against that tree and must
32	// decide dormancy by the same test that repo's own scheduler used. A second notion of
33	// dormancy would nag exactly the repos that had already opted out.
34	//
35	// Import-light and free of `node:` on purpose: the dashboard page reads this in the
36	// browser through the pack's published shared-code/, and a `node:` import anywhere in
37	// that graph blocks the page's first module load.
38	import { RENAMED_PACKS } from '../../engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs';
39	
40	// Whose parameter this is. Exported because a reader that has to name the pack to find
41	// its config should name it from here rather than spell the id a second time.
42	export const TASKS_PACK_ID = 'claudinite-tasks';
43	
44	// A declared id as it resolves today. A member's declaration can carry a spelling from
45	// before a rename, and the config of a pack a member writes into its own repo must keep
46	// resolving under every spelling it was ever written under.
47	const resolves = (id) => typeof id === 'string' && (RENAMED_PACKS[id] ?? id) === TASKS_PACK_ID;
48	
49	// This pack's parameters, from whichever shape the caller holds.
50	//
51	// The normalized view first: `loadConfig` folds every entry's `config` into `packConfig`
52	// keyed by the pack's own id, so a scheduler that already loaded its settings needs no
53	// second walk. Then the raw declaration, where the parameters sit on the entry object as
54	// the member wrote them — which is all a cross-repo reader ever has.
55	function packParameters(config) {
56	  if (config === null || typeof config !== 'object') return undefined;
57	  const folded = undefined;
58	  if (folded !== null && typeof folded === 'object') return folded;
59	  for (const entry of Array.isArray(config.packs) ? config.packs : []) {
60	    if (entry !== null && typeof entry === 'object' && resolves(entry.id)) return entry.config;
61	  }
62	  return undefined;
63	}
64	
65	// What the declaration says, before any judgement about whether it says it legally.
66	// `undefined` means the project never answered, which is the normal shape and means awake.
67	function declared(config) {
68	  if (config === null || typeof config !== 'object') return undefined;
69	  const own = packParameters(config)?.dormant;
70	  if (own !== undefined) return own;
71	  // The retired spelling, underneath the pack entry so a converged member is never
72	  // overridden by a stale key its migration left behind. `raw` is the declaration as
73	  // the member wrote it, which is where a top-level key survives now that the engine
74	  // no longer normalizes one it does not own.
75	  // @legacy-tolerance advisory:legacy-shape-in-use retire:#1846
76	  return config.raw?.dormant ?? config.dormant;
77	}
78	
79	// The predicate. Strictly `=== true`, so every malformed value below reads as awake —
80	// the conservative direction, since the alternative is silently stopping a project's
81	// entire scheduled workload on a typo.
82	export const isDormant = (config) => declared(config) === true;
83	
84	// The settings errors this parameter can carry, in the `{ what, fix }` shape the world
85	// runner collects. A string "true", a `{ since }` object or a reason left in its place
86	// would all read as dormant to a truthiness test and as awake to the predicate above,
87	// and the difference is a whole repo's scheduled work — so the wrong TYPE is reported
88	// rather than coerced. The pack owns this because the pack owns the parameter.
89	export function dormancyErrors(config) {
90	  const value = declared(config);
91	  if (value === undefined || typeof value === 'boolean') return [];
92	  return [{
93	    what: `"dormant" on the "${TASKS_PACK_ID}" pack entry must be true or false, got ${JSON.stringify(value)}`,
94	    fix: `set it to true to stop this project's recurring work, or remove it — e.g. { "id": "${TASKS_PACK_ID}", "config": { "dormant": true } }`,
95	  }];
96	}

1	// The FRESHNESS half of the fleet-roster sweep: the `fleet-drift` issue family, the
2	// root-cause classification behind it, and the freshness section of the run report.
3	//
4	// It holds no enumeration and no membership classification — the roster is built once,
5	// for both halves, by its sibling check-fleet-roster.mjs, which hands this module only
6	// the members it has already established are covered, awake, in scope and this sweep's
7	// to measure. What lives here is everything specific to the freshness QUESTION. Its
8	// counterpart is adoption-issues.mjs, which owns the same three things for the coverage
9	// question; the two never import each other.
10	//
11	// WHY THE QUESTION EXISTS. Under per-project scheduling every member maintains ITSELF:
12	// its own vendored `claudinite-scheduler.yml` fires hourly, and its `baselining` task
13	// re-vendors the mount from canon. That is the right architecture — and it removed the
14	// last thing that ever looked at a member from the outside. A member whose scheduler
15	// was never vendored, whose workflow was deleted, or whose baselining has been failing
